# Dunmore Tannery Works Manual

## Yard and pit practice

- Hides arriving at the Dunmore tannery are weighed on the yard scale before anything else, and the green weight is chalked on the flank and copied into the receiving ledger. A hide under 18 kilograms green is set aside for the calf pits and never mixed with the heavy ox hides, because the strong liquors that suit an ox hide will burn a calf skin in a single night. The yard foreman signs the ledger for every delivery, and any hide with a brand cut deeper than the grain is photographed for the drover's claim before it goes near the soak. Salted hides are shaken free of the old salt on the grating and the salt swept into the barrow for the road gritting in winter, never into the drain where it would kill the bacteria in the effluent pond.
- The lime pits are charged on Tuesdays with 90 kilograms of slaked lime and 4 kilograms of sodium sulphide to the pit, and the hides are handled in the lime for exactly ten days with a stir each morning. A pit that has stood longer than twelve days produces grain that cracks at the fold, so the foreman marks the loading date on the pit board in chalk and the liming gang reads the board before touching a pit. The pit lids are kept shut between stirs because the vapour is harmful, and no one works over a lime pit alone; a second man always stands at the rail with the rope and the lifebuoy.
- Fleshing and scudding are done on the beam by hand at Dunmore, never by machine, because the machine knives have a habit of scoring the thin flanks, and the fleshings are carted every afternoon to the glue boilers at Corrow. The beam men are paid by the dozen hides and sharpen their own knives on the stone at the end of the shed. A bad cut is not hidden: the man calls the foreman, the hide is chalked with a cross, and it goes to the cheap shoe-sole grade instead of the saddlery bench.
- The bark liquors are made up from ground oak bark in the leaching tubs, and the strongest liquor, the one the hides finish in, is held at a gravity of 14 degrees on the Barkometer. The handlers move hides up through the pits from the weakest to the strongest over twelve weeks, and the tanning master tests the liquor with the hydrometer every morning and records the reading. If the gravity is allowed to climb above the mark the grain draws and hardens, and a draw grain can never be cured; the whole pit is then sold off as rough butts at half price.
- The drying loft is opened at first light and closed at dusk and the vents are set by the loftman according to the wind, never by the thermometer. Hides hang for at least nine days in summer and fourteen in winter before they are brought down for the currier. The loftman keeps the loft keys on his belt and signs the book for every hide he lets out, since leather lifted from a loft in the damp season is the commonest cause of mould in the bale and the quarrels that follow with the saddlers.
